title: Ship a service from commit to cluster
summary: Take one small web service from a laptop to a running Kubernetes deployment, with a container, a pipeline, infrastructure as code and a rollback you have tried.
who: Anyone aiming at a DevOps engineer role who wants one finished project to show.
needs: A laptop with Docker and a free Git host account. Everything runs locally with kind, so no cloud bill.
outcome: A repository with a tested service, a hardened image, a CI pipeline, a Terraform module, a Kubernetes manifest set and a written rollback.

stages.title: Write the service and its tests
stages.goal: A small HTTP service with a health endpoint and three tests that run in under ten seconds.
build: Create a repository with a service in any language you know: GET /healthz, GET /items, POST /items.
Add three tests: health returns 200, create then list returns the item, bad input returns 400.
Add a Makefile with test, run and lint targets so every later stage calls the same commands.
check: make test passes from a clean clone
The service starts with one command and answers /healthz
The repository has a README with the run and test commands
stages.keep: The repository, with the Makefile and the tests.

breakit.do: Change the POST /items handler so bad input returns 200 instead of 400, then run make test.
breakit.see: The bad-input test fails and make test exits non-zero. If it still passes, your test was not testing that case.
breakit.fix: Restore the 400, then add a test for an empty body so the gap cannot return.

stages.title: Package it as a small, safe image
stages.goal: A multi-stage image that runs as a non-root user and starts in under a second.
build: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile: build in one stage, copy only the result into a slim final stage.
Set a non-root USER, a HEALTHCHECK and a read-only root filesystem when you run it.
Add a .dockerignore and order layers so a code change does not reinstall dependencies.
Write a compose file with the service and a database, and bring it up with one command.
check: docker run --read-only starts the service
docker image ls shows the final image well under the build image size
Rebuilding after a one-line code change reuses the dependency layer
stages.keep: Dockerfile, .dockerignore and compose.yaml in the repository.

breakit.do: Delete the USER line from the Dockerfile, rebuild, and run: docker run --rm IMAGE id -u
breakit.see: It prints 0: the service now runs as root inside the container.
breakit.fix: Put USER back. Add a pipeline step that fails when id -u prints 0.

stages.title: Build the pipeline
stages.goal: A pipeline that tests, builds and pushes the image on every push, and blocks a bad change.
build: Create a pipeline with three jobs: test, build image, push image. The push job runs only on the main branch.
Tag images with the commit hash, never only latest.
Store registry credentials as pipeline secrets and keep them out of logs.
Add a vulnerability scan of the image and fail the job on a critical finding.
Open a pull request that breaks a test and confirm the pipeline blocks it.
check: A failing test stops the pipeline before the image is built
The pushed image is tagged with the commit hash
No secret value appears in any job log
stages.keep: The pipeline file and a link to one green and one red run.

breakit.do: Pin the base image to an old tag with a known critical vulnerability and push a branch.
breakit.see: The scan job fails and the image is never pushed.
breakit.fix: Move to a patched tag and pin it by version. Keep the scan as a required check.

stages.title: Describe the infrastructure as code
stages.goal: A Terraform module that creates the cluster and namespace the service runs in.
build: Write a Terraform module that creates a kind cluster (or a namespace on one you already have) from variables.
Expose the cluster name and kubeconfig path as outputs.
Run plan, apply, then plan again and confirm the second plan shows no changes.
Change one variable, read the plan, and apply it.
Destroy it and recreate it from scratch to prove nothing was done by hand.
check: The second plan reports no changes
Destroy and apply recreates the cluster with no manual steps
State is not committed to the repository
stages.keep: infra/ directory with the module, a variables example and a short README.

breakit.do: Change something by hand on the cluster, for example label the namespace with kubectl label, then run terraform plan.
breakit.see: The plan shows the difference between the code and the real cluster (drift).
breakit.fix: Decide which side is right: apply to remove the label, or add it to the code. Never leave drift unexplained.

stages.title: Deploy to Kubernetes
stages.goal: The service running as a Deployment behind a Service, with probes, limits and configuration.
build: Write a Deployment with three replicas, readiness and liveness probes on /healthz, and CPU and memory requests and limits.
Add a Service and an Ingress or port-forward, and reach the service from outside the pod.
Move configuration into a ConfigMap and the database password into a Secret.
Kill a pod and watch the Deployment replace it without dropped requests.
Add the apply step to the pipeline for the main branch.
check: kubectl rollout status finishes cleanly
Deleting a pod causes no failed requests while two others serve
No credential is written in plain text in a manifest
stages.keep: k8s/ directory with the manifests, applied by the pipeline.

breakit.do: Change the readiness probe path to /nope and apply the Deployment.
breakit.see: The new pods never become Ready and the rollout stalls. The old pods keep serving traffic.
breakit.fix: Restore the path, or run kubectl rollout undo. Note how the probe protected users.

stages.title: Roll out, break it and roll back
stages.goal: A rolling update, a deliberately bad release, and a rollback you can do in under two minutes.
build: Release version 2 with a rolling update and watch old and new pods overlap.
Release a version 3 that fails its readiness probe and confirm traffic stays on version 2.
Roll back with kubectl rollout undo and time it.
Write a one-page runbook: how to see what changed, how to roll back, how to confirm recovery.
Add a feature flag so one behaviour can be switched off without a deploy.
check: A bad release never receives traffic
Rollback restores the previous version in under two minutes
The runbook lets someone else do the rollback without you
stages.keep: RUNBOOK.md in the repository and a short description of what you would change next.

breakit.do: Release a version that needs an environment variable you have not defined, such as DB_URL.
breakit.see: Pods enter CrashLoopBackOff and the logs name the missing variable.
breakit.fix: Roll back first with kubectl rollout undo, then add the key to the ConfigMap and release again.

title: Run a service reliably
summary: Define reliability for a small service, measure it, alert on it, break it on purpose and write up what happened, the way an SRE team works.
who: Anyone aiming at an SRE role, or an engineer who now carries a pager.
needs: Docker and Docker Compose on a laptop. Prometheus and Grafana run locally from containers.
outcome: A service with written SLOs, working metrics and burn-rate alerts, an on-call runbook, a game-day report and a postmortem.
tools: a load generator such as hey or k6

stages.title: Pick the user journeys and write SLOs
stages.goal: Two SLIs and two SLOs with an error budget in minutes, agreed in writing.
build: Run a small web service with Compose (any service with a database works).
List the two journeys users care about most and write an SLI for each: for example, requests under 300 ms and non-error responses.
Set SLO targets, for example 99.5 percent over 28 days, and convert each to an error budget in minutes.
Write down what the team does when the budget is spent.
check: Each SLI is a ratio of good events to valid events
The error budget is stated in minutes and in requests
The budget policy says who decides and what stops
stages.keep: SLO.md with SLIs, targets, budget and policy.

breakit.do: Set your SLO target to 100 percent and work out the error budget.
breakit.see: The budget is zero minutes, so a single failed request breaches the SLO.
breakit.fix: Choose a target the users would not notice missing, such as 99.5 percent, and write down why 100 percent is not a goal.

stages.title: Instrument and measure
stages.goal: Prometheus scraping request rate, errors and latency, with a Grafana dashboard per journey.
build: Expose request count, error count and a latency histogram from the service.
Run Prometheus and Grafana beside it and confirm the targets are up.
Build a dashboard with rate, errors and p95 latency, and a panel for remaining error budget.
Switch the service to structured logs with a request id on every line.
Generate load and watch the graphs move.
check: The dashboard shows the SLI exactly as SLO.md defines it
Logs carry a request id you can follow across lines
Cardinality is bounded: no user id or URL path as a label
stages.keep: Dashboard JSON and the Prometheus config in the repository.

breakit.do: Add the user id as a metric label and send requests with 1,000 different ids.
breakit.see: The number of time series jumps (check prometheus_tsdb_head_series) and Prometheus memory grows.
breakit.fix: Remove the label. Keep the id in logs, where high cardinality is cheap.

stages.title: Alert on burn rate, not noise
stages.goal: Two burn-rate alerts, a fast one and a slow one, each with a link to a runbook.
build: Write a fast alert (burning budget about 14 times too fast over one hour) and a slow alert (about 2 times over three days).
Route the fast alert to a page and the slow alert to a ticket.
Write a runbook per alert: what it means, how to check, how to fix, when to escalate.
Trigger each alert by injecting errors and confirm only the right one fires.
check: A short error spike does not page anyone
A sustained burn pages within minutes
Every alert links to a runbook that names a first command to run
stages.keep: Alert rules and one runbook per alert.

breakit.do: Set the fast alert to fire at a 1x burn rate and inject a short burst of errors.
breakit.see: The alert pages for a spike that cost almost no budget: this is noise.
breakit.fix: Restore the multi-window thresholds so only a sustained burn pages.

stages.title: Make it resilient
stages.goal: Timeouts, retries with backoff and a health-based restart, shown to work under failure.
build: Add a timeout to every outbound call and retries with exponential backoff and jitter, capped.
Add a circuit breaker or a load-shed rule for an overloaded dependency.
Run a load test to the point of failure and note the requests per second where latency breaks the SLO.
Write a short production readiness checklist and score your service against it.
check: A slow dependency does not take the whole service down
You can state the capacity limit as a number
The readiness checklist has no unanswered item
stages.keep: Load test results and the readiness checklist.

breakit.do: Remove the timeout on one outbound call and make the dependency answer after 30 seconds.
breakit.see: Workers pile up waiting, the whole service stops answering and the latency SLI collapses.
breakit.fix: Restore the timeout, cap the retries and add a circuit breaker.

stages.title: Run a game day
stages.goal: A planned failure exercise with a hypothesis, a stop rule and a written result.
build: Write a hypothesis: for example, if the database is killed, the service degrades gracefully and recovers in under two minutes.
Define the stop rule before you start and who can call it.
Inject the failure: stop the database container, add 500 ms of latency, or fill the disk.
Record what you saw against the hypothesis and what surprised you.
Restore the database from a backup and time the restore.
check: The hypothesis and stop rule were written before the test
The restore was actually performed and timed
At least one surprise led to a change
stages.keep: GAMEDAY.md with hypothesis, timeline and result.

breakit.do: Delete the latest backup file, then try the restore from your runbook.
breakit.see: The restore fails. This is the lesson: an untested backup is not a backup.
breakit.fix: Add a scheduled job that restores into a scratch database and checks a row count.

stages.title: Write the postmortem
stages.goal: A blameless postmortem of the game day with a timeline, causes and tracked actions.
build: Write a timeline in UTC from the first symptom to full recovery.
List contributing causes, not a single root cause, and avoid naming a person as the cause.
Write three actions, each with an owner and a date, and at least one that removes toil.
Write the status update you would have sent to users during the incident.
Review how much error budget the incident would have used.
check: The postmortem names no individual as the cause
Every action has an owner and a date
The budget impact is stated against SLO.md
stages.keep: POSTMORTEM.md and the status update draft.

breakit.do: Rewrite one postmortem action as "be more careful next time" and review it against your own rules.
breakit.see: It has no owner, no date and no way to tell if it is done.
breakit.fix: Rewrite it as a change to a system, with an owner and a date.

title: Operate a Kubernetes cluster
summary: Build a cluster, deliver apps with Helm and Argo CD, lock it down, back up etcd and rehearse a restore.
who: Anyone preparing for the CKA or taking on cluster operations.
needs: A laptop that can run kind or minikube with three nodes, or a free-tier virtual machine.
outcome: A multi-node cluster with delivered apps, access control, network policy, quotas, a tested etcd restore and an upgrade plan.

stages.title: Stand up the cluster
stages.goal: A three-node cluster and a clear picture of what runs the control plane.
build: Create a cluster with one control plane node and two workers using a kind config file.
List the control plane components and find where each runs and where its logs are.
Find the etcd data directory and the certificate paths.
Label the workers and schedule a pod to one using nodeSelector.
check: You can name each control plane component and what it does
kubectl get nodes shows three Ready nodes
The cluster config is a file in the repository, not a command history
stages.keep: cluster.yaml and notes on the control plane.

breakit.do: In the control plane node, move kube-apiserver.yaml out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests for a minute.
breakit.see: kubectl is refused or times out, but pods already running keep running.
breakit.fix: Move the file back and watch the API server return. Note what the control plane does and does not do for running pods.

stages.title: Deliver apps with Helm and Argo CD
stages.goal: An app installed from a chart and kept in sync from a Git repository.
build: Write a small chart with a Deployment, a Service and values for dev and prod.
Install Argo CD and create an Application that points at the chart in your repository.
Change a value in Git and watch Argo CD sync it.
Edit the live Deployment by hand and watch Argo CD report drift and fix it.
Roll back by reverting the commit.
check: Argo CD shows Synced and Healthy
A manual change is reverted automatically
Reverting the commit restores the previous state
stages.keep: charts/ and the Application manifest.

breakit.do: Commit a chart with a template syntax error and let Argo CD pick it up.
breakit.see: Argo CD shows a comparison error and the live app is untouched.
breakit.fix: Revert the commit. Add helm lint and helm template to the pipeline so it fails before merge.

stages.title: Control who can do what
stages.goal: Role-based access for two teams and a service account with only the rights it needs.
build: Create two namespaces, team-a and team-b.
Write a Role and RoleBinding that let team-a edit only its own namespace.
Use kubectl auth can-i with --as to prove team-a cannot read team-b.
Create a service account for an app with read access to one ConfigMap and nothing else.
Enable Pod Security admission at the restricted level on one namespace and fix a failing pod.
check: can-i answers match the policy you wrote
No workload uses the default service account
A privileged pod is refused in the restricted namespace
stages.keep: rbac/ manifests and a table of who can do what.

breakit.do: Bind team-a to cluster-admin "just to test", then run kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n team-b --as team-a-user.
breakit.see: It answers yes: team-a can read team-b secrets.
breakit.fix: Remove the binding. Add a can-i check script that runs on every change.

stages.title: Isolate and share fairly
stages.goal: Default-deny network policy and quotas so one team cannot starve another.
build: Apply a default-deny ingress policy to team-a, then allow only the frontend to reach the API.
Test that a pod from team-b cannot reach team-a and that the frontend can.
Add a ResourceQuota and a LimitRange to each namespace.
Create a workload that exceeds the quota and read the refusal message.
Add a HorizontalPodAutoscaler and drive load until it scales.
check: Cross-namespace traffic is blocked unless allowed
A quota breach is refused with a clear message
The autoscaler adds and then removes replicas
stages.keep: policies/ and quota manifests.

breakit.do: Delete the default-deny NetworkPolicy from team-a and curl its API from a team-b pod.
breakit.see: The request succeeds: the namespace is open again.
breakit.fix: Reapply the policy and turn the curl into an automated test.

stages.title: Back up and restore etcd
stages.goal: A snapshot taken on a schedule and a restore you have done and timed.
build: Create a few objects, then take an etcd snapshot with etcdctl and verify it with snapshot status.
Delete a namespace and its workloads.
Restore the snapshot into a new data directory and point the control plane at it.
Confirm the objects are back and note how long it took.
Write the runbook, including where the snapshot is stored and who has access.
check: The snapshot passes verification
The deleted objects were restored from it
The runbook was followed by you start to finish
stages.keep: DR-RUNBOOK.md with timings.

breakit.do: Truncate a copy of your snapshot with head -c 1000 and run etcdutl snapshot status on it.
breakit.see: The status check fails: a damaged snapshot looks like a file until you check it.
breakit.fix: Verify every snapshot after taking it and copy it off the node.

stages.title: Upgrade and debug
stages.goal: A written upgrade plan, one node drained and upgraded, and three faults found and fixed.
build: Write an upgrade plan: version skew rules, order of nodes, rollback point and checks after each step.
Cordon and drain a worker, confirm pods moved and PodDisruptionBudgets were respected, then uncordon.
Break three things on purpose (wrong image tag, failing probe, a node NotReady) and fix each from symptoms only.
Record the commands you used to diagnose each fault.
check: The plan says what to check before and after each node
Drain respected the disruption budget
Each fault was found from events and logs, not by guessing
stages.keep: UPGRADE.md and the fault notes.

breakit.do: Create a PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable equal to the replica count, then drain the node.
breakit.see: The drain blocks and keeps retrying because no pod may be evicted.
breakit.fix: Raise the replicas or relax the budget for the drain, then restore it.

title: Build a secure cloud landing zone
summary: Design accounts, identity, networking, encryption, logging and cost controls as code, then test them by trying to break them.
who: Anyone aiming at a cloud engineer role on AWS or Azure.
needs: A free-tier cloud account, Terraform, and billing alerts switched on before you start.
outcome: A Terraform-defined foundation with least-privilege roles, a private network, encrypted storage, audit logging, guardrails and a cost budget.

stages.title: Plan accounts and guardrails
stages.goal: A written layout of accounts or subscriptions and the rules that apply to all of them.
build: Draw the layout: management, security and logging, shared services, and one workload account per environment.
Write the guardrails: no public storage, only approved regions, logging cannot be switched off.
Set a monthly budget with alerts at 50, 80 and 100 percent before creating anything.
Choose a tagging scheme: owner, environment, cost-centre.
check: The layout explains why each account exists
Each guardrail is written as a testable statement
The budget alert exists before any resource
stages.keep: DESIGN.md with the diagram, guardrails and tags.

breakit.do: Pick the guardrail "no public storage" and write the single command that would break it.
breakit.see: You now have a test case ready for stage 4. Without a test, a guardrail is only a wish.
breakit.fix: Record the command and the expected denial in DESIGN.md.

stages.title: Identity with least privilege
stages.goal: Roles instead of long-lived keys, and a policy you reduced from broad to narrow.
build: Create a role for a deployment pipeline that can only deploy to one account.
Let the pipeline assume the role through OIDC so no access key is stored anywhere.
Start from a broad policy, run the access analyzer or policy simulator, and cut it down to what is used.
Turn on MFA for human users and remove any unused access keys.
check: No long-lived key exists for the pipeline
The final policy names actions and resources, not wildcards
A denied action returns the error you expected
stages.keep: iam/ Terraform and the before and after policies.

breakit.do: In a sandbox account, attach full administrator rights to the pipeline role, then run the policy analyzer.
breakit.see: The analyzer reports wide, unused permissions on the role.
breakit.fix: Replace it with the scoped policy and add an alert for any administrator attachment.

stages.title: A private network
stages.goal: A VPC or virtual network with public and private subnets and no open admin ports.
build: Define the network in Terraform with CIDR ranges that leave room for growth and do not overlap other networks.
Place workloads in private subnets and reach the internet through a NAT or egress rule.
Allow administration through a managed session service, not an open SSH port.
Add private endpoints for storage so traffic stays off the internet.
Prove it: scan your own address space and confirm no admin port is reachable.
check: No security group or rule allows 0.0.0.0/0 to an admin port
Storage is reached over a private endpoint
CIDR ranges are documented and do not overlap
stages.keep: network/ Terraform and the CIDR table.

breakit.do: In a sandbox, open port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 on a security group and run your configuration check.
breakit.see: The check flags an open admin port.
breakit.fix: Remove the rule and use the managed session service. Keep the check as a scheduled test.

stages.title: Protect the data
stages.goal: Encrypted storage with customer-managed keys, versioning and a lifecycle rule.
build: Create a storage bucket or account with public access blocked, versioning on and encryption using your own key.
Write a key policy that lets only one role decrypt.
Add a lifecycle rule that moves old data to cheaper storage and expires it later.
Store an application secret in a secrets manager and read it from a workload without writing it to disk.
Check that no secret appears in Terraform state or in plan output.
check: Public access is blocked at account level
Only the named role can use the key
State and logs contain no secret value
stages.keep: data/ Terraform with the key and lifecycle policy.

breakit.do: In a sandbox, switch off the bucket public access block and upload a harmless test file with a public setting.
breakit.see: Your guardrail or config rule flags it, and the test file is reachable from outside.
breakit.fix: Switch the block back on and add the account-level guardrail that denies the change.

stages.title: See everything
stages.goal: Audit logs on, centralised, protected from deletion and searchable.
build: Enable the account audit trail in every region and send it to a bucket in the logging account.
Make the log bucket write-once or deny deletion for everyone except a break-glass role.
Create an alert for three events: root login, a policy change and a disabled trail.
Trigger each event on purpose and confirm the alert arrives.
Write the query you would run first after a suspected key leak.
check: The trail covers all regions
Nobody in the workload account can delete the logs
Each alert fired when you triggered it
stages.keep: logging/ Terraform and the alert tests.

breakit.do: In a sandbox, stop the audit trail for a few minutes, then start it again.
breakit.see: Your "trail disabled" alert fires and the logs show a gap.
breakit.fix: Add a guardrail that denies stopping the trail except for the break-glass role.

stages.title: Control cost and recover
stages.goal: A cost report by tag, one rightsizing change and a tested recovery from a lost environment.
build: Break down the bill by your tags and find any untagged spend.
Pick the largest resource, check its real use, and change its size.
Destroy the workload environment and recreate it from Terraform alone, timing it.
Run a plan and fix any drift between the code and the real resources.
Write down your recovery time and what is not yet covered.
check: Untagged spend is zero or explained
The environment was rebuilt from code only
The recovery time is a measured number
stages.keep: COST-AND-RECOVERY.md with the numbers.

breakit.do: In a sandbox, create one resource with no tags and wait for the next cost report.
breakit.see: It appears under untagged spend.
breakit.fix: Add a tag policy that blocks untagged creation, and an automatic stop for dev resources.
